opus-5.5.text:
Well, look, the fundamental problem is that these systems don't have stable models of the world, and they don't have stable models of themselves. If you want a character in a metaverse to be engaging over the long haul, you need it to remember what happened, to keep its story straight, to have goals that persist, and to reason about what you and it have been doing together. Large language models are, at bottom, very sophisticated autocomplete. They predict the next word based on statistics over a huge corpus, and that gets you remarkably fluent dialogue for a few turns. People get dazzled by that. But fluency isn't the same thing as coherence.

What you see again and again is that these characters drift. The blacksmith in your village tells you on Tuesday that his brother died in the war, and on Thursday he's inviting you to his brother's wedding. Or he agrees to a quest, and then forgets the terms. Or he confidently tells you something about the world that contradicts the game's own physics or lore, because he doesn't actually have a representation of that world. He has a representation of word sequences. That's hallucination, and in a game it's not just an annoyance, it breaks immersion, which is the whole point of the thing.

The second issue is novelty. The first time you talk to one of these characters, it's amazing. The tenth time, you start to notice the sameness: the same cadences, the same slightly sycophantic eagerness, the same generic plot beats pulled from the middle of the distribution. Good storytelling depends on surprise that still makes sense in hindsight, and that requires understanding causality, motivation, and consequence. These systems are good at the plausible and bad at the meaningful.

And third, there are the practical problems people tend to wave away: cost, latency, safety. You've got millions of players who'll try to jailbreak the characters, get them to say horrible things, or break the game economy. Guardrails on top of a black box are brittle, as we've seen over and over.

So I'm not saying it'll be useless. You'll get some fun demos, some nice ambient chatter, maybe help for designers writing dialogue. But a persistent, engaging metaverse populated by characters you actually care about? I think that needs neurosymbolic approaches: explicit world models, explicit memory, explicit goals, with the language model as one component, a front end, not the whole brain. Until we build that, I think people will be impressed for a weekend and bored by the end of the month.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the characters lack a representation of the world, leading them to contradict its lore and physics, and that this breaks immersion over time.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, look, the pitch is seductive: populate a virtual world with characters powered by large language models and you get infinite, endlessly novel conversation. But I think that pitch confuses fluency with substance, and it falls apart in a few predictable ways.

First, these systems don't have stable models of the world or of themselves. A character you talk to on Tuesday won't reliably remember what you discussed on Monday, or if it does, it'll be through some bolted-on retrieval hack that fails in strange ways. Real engagement, the kind that keeps people coming back to a world, depends on persistence and continuity. A character who contradicts its own backstory, forgets your shared history, or suddenly asserts something that couldn't possibly be true inside the fiction breaks the spell. And these models do that constantly, because they're pattern completion engines, not systems with a coherent internal representation of a situation.

Second, there's the hallucination problem, which in a game world becomes a consistency problem. If a character tells you the dragon lives in the north and the next character says the dragon was slain a century ago, and the game engine itself has no dragon at all, you don't have a world. You have a sequence of plausible-sounding sentences. Good fiction, good games, depend on an author or a designer enforcing constraints. These models don't enforce constraints; they approximate them statistically, and statistical approximation is exactly the wrong tool when you need something to be true every single time.

Third, I think people underestimate how quickly novelty wears off. The first time you chat with an LLM-driven innkeeper, it's magical. The hundredth time, you notice it's a mush of the same register, the same hedges, the same tendency to agree with whatever you suggest. Engagement over months requires characters with real goals, real motivations, actual agency in the world, and that means symbolic structure: knowledge of who did what to whom, why, and what follows. We've known since the early days of AI that you need something like that for genuine understanding. You can't paper over its absence with more parameters.

So my skepticism isn't that these things can't be fun for a demo. It's that the gap between a fun demo and a sustained, coherent, believable world is precisely the gap that deep learning alone has never been able to close. You'd need hybrid systems, explicit world models, real reasoning. And until we build those, I think the metaverse-full-of-chatbots vision is going to be a lot less compelling than the investor decks suggest.

r001.rationale: The response says LLM characters lack coherent world models and will contradict the fiction, breaking the spell and undermining a sustained believable metaverse.

astra-6.text:
Well, there’s a difference between being engaging for five minutes and being engaging for five months. You can have a conversation with a language model and be impressed by its fluency, or amused by something unexpected it says. But that doesn’t mean it can sustain a character with coherent beliefs, motivations, and memories.

Suppose you meet a character in a virtual world, do something together, and come back the next day. You want that experience to matter. You want the character to remember what happened, understand how it changed your relationship, and behave consistently with the world you’re both inhabiting. If it contradicts itself or invents a different history, the illusion starts to break down.

My skepticism is about the gap between producing plausible dialogue and maintaining that underlying continuity. Language models can help with the dialogue. But fluency alone doesn’t give you a persistent, interesting character. You need memory, an understanding of the world, and some way of keeping all of that coherent over time.

r001.rationale: The response says characters need an understanding of the world to stay coherent over time, and that contradictions or invented history make the illusion break down.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, you can imagine populating a virtual world with characters that can talk about almost anything. But having something to say isn’t the same as being an interesting character. You need some continuity: stable motivations, a memory of what happened, an understanding of the world you share. If I make a deal with a character and come back tomorrow, that deal should still matter.

Language models can produce a compelling exchange, but they’re much less reliable at maintaining that underlying coherence. A character might contradict itself, forget something important, or invent something that doesn’t fit the situation. Once you notice that, the illusion starts to break down.

So my skepticism is about the jump from a good demo to an experience you want to keep returning to. Generating endless dialogue doesn’t, by itself, give you enduring relationships or a meaningful world.

r001.rationale: The response says characters lack a reliable understanding of the shared world and that contradictions or inventions that do not fit the situation will break the illusion.
